title: Pin a crimped contact into cavity 3 until the locking fingers click, prove it with a tug, then fit the secondary lock
instruction: Push the crimped contact into cavity 3 of the connector, as on the pinout card, from the wire side, until it clicks; hold the housing with one hand and push the wire close behind the crimp with the other. Tug the wire lightly to check it is locked, then push the secondary lock fully into the housing's mating face. Then let go of everything.
context: Robot building: robot arms, mobile bases and humanoids are wired with harnesses of crimped contacts pinned into sealed connector housings, cavity by cavity from a pinout, and wire-harness production remains one of the most manual areas of manufacturing (Automotive Manufacturing Solutions, Sep 2026). Sealed 4-way size-16 connectors such as TE's DEUTSCH DT family (cable-to-cable and cable-to-device, 13 A per contact) can carry the power and signal runs between a robot's battery, motor drives and sensors. A robot that can pin a contact by pinout, prove it with a tug and fit the secondary lock can help build the harnesses of the next robots. A contact that has not clicked in looks inserted but backs out when the connector is mated: a classic harness fault, caught by a tug and by the secondary lock.
setup: All positions from the arm bases' midline (x forward, y left). On the table: a black sealed 4-way connector housing (glass-filled nylon, 24 mm wide x 40 mm long x 24 mm tall) lying on its side, loose, its rear face (wire side) at x 0.30 m, y 0.02 m facing -y (toward the right arm); four square cavities 3.9 mm across, 10 mm apart, numbered 1-4 by moulded dots as seen from the rear (1 top left, 2 top right, 3 bottom right, 4 bottom left), each with a 6 mm lead-in funnel; on its mating face (the front, facing +y) four 1.1 mm channels (2.3 mm at the face) beside the columns of cavities run 22 mm back to the locking fingers. A crimped size-16 socket contact (gold, 21 mm, shoulder 3.8 mm across) on a red 1.0 mm2 wire (2.6 mm across, 140 mm, free end) lies on a grey two-block rest (20 mm tall, a 38 mm gap behind the crimp) at x 0.305 m, its crimp end at y -0.09 m, nose toward the housing. An orange secondary lock (a wedgelock: a 26 x 22 x 6 mm face plate with four wedge blades 0.8 x 16 x 22 mm) stands blades-down in the pocket of a grey 24 x 34 x 26 mm holder, its plate on the rim, at x 0.22 m, y 0.17 m. A white 50 x 36 mm pinout card at x 0.19 m, y 0.10 m shows the cavities as seen from the rear, cavity 3 red. A 2 mm white reference band is printed on the wire, its centre 15 mm behind the crimp end (seated: 3.9 mm outside the rear face). Real trial: a TE DEUTSCH DT06-4S 4-way plug, a W4S wedgelock (the secondary lock) and a 0462-201-16141 size-16 socket contact (sold together as a DT06-4S kit) crimped with an IWISS IWD-1620 size-16 solid-contact crimper ($24.99; or a DEUTSCH HDT-48-00) onto 140 mm of red 18 AWG automotive wire, the white band painted 15 mm behind the crimp end; the pinout card marks the cavity moulded 3 on the plug's rear grommet.
scoring: In cavity 3 = the contact's nose at least 5 mm into cavity 3 from the rear, on its axis (within 1 mm), pointing in (within 20 degrees). Locked = three observable checks: (a) mark: the wire's white band within 1.0 mm of its seated position, measured with a ruler from the rear face (real trial: the seated position is measured once on a reference contact whose wedgelock went home); (b) the robot's own tug: with the contact clicked, a hand closed on the wire within 60 mm of the crimp draws it back along the cavity for at least 0.5 s while the other hand holds the housing (simulation: every fingertip of that hand within 8 mm of the wire and the contact drawn 0.15-1 mm back from its seated depth onto its fingers; real trial: video shows the wire taut in line with the cavity and the mark moving under 1 mm); (c) the independent retention test: once no fingertip has been within 25 mm of the contact or the first 60 mm of wire for 1 s, 30 N on the wire against the housing (ramped 1 s, held 0.5 s); it holds if the contact (the mark) moves under 1 mm (real trial: done after the run ends, so the robot's run is not disturbed: spring scale, housing in a soft-jaw vise; the wedgelock only goes home over clicked contacts, so the result matches). Lock in = the secondary lock fully home with every finger closed: simulation, the wedgelock's plate flat on the mating face within 0.3 mm, square and centred, its blades in the channels; real trial, the W4S pushed into the plug's mating face until it snaps and sits flush (a straightedge across the face leaves no gap a 0.3 mm feeler gauge enters). Score: 1.0 (success) = in cavity 3, locked, lock in, no fingertip within 20 mm of housing, contact, wire or lock for 1 s, all still; 0.75 = same, still touched; 0.5 = in cavity 3 and locked, lock not in; 0.25 = in cavity 3 only (including no robot tug); 0 = otherwise, or (latched) the contact ever locked in another cavity, or the lock pushed in until its blades reach the fingers (plate within 2.0 mm of the mating face) while a contact was in but not clicked, or a blade loaded 20 N (housing damaged).
reset_notes: Pull the contact out with an extraction tool (the fingers hold it), pull the wedgelock out of the mating face and stand it back, blades down, in its holder; housing, contact on its rest and card as in the screenshot. A housing with a forced secondary lock must be replaced.
fidelity: CPU PhysX, 240 Hz. Own parts sized like a DT06-4S plug, W4S and size-16 contact. Wire: 10 mm links, bending springs. Each cavity: two sprung fingers (4 N/mm) that click behind the shoulder. Simplified: clicked fingers are held shut; the simulated retention test is 8 N (a held contact counts as passing 30 N); the robot's tug is read from the contact's position; the wedgelock enters the mating face like the W4S but is a plain plate with blades, no snap; forcing it is judged by position and load.
